items.title: The dashboard's three “in-step progress” fields are all derived values: progress has a maximum error of 0 seconds, expected is the median of the last 3 steps, and gen_frac is the previous step's generation fraction and is frozen for the entire step
items.summary: Of the four fields on the dashboard that show “how far this step has gotten,” only since and phase are real-time observations in practice. progress is exactly equal to min(1, since/expected), with error 0 at 27 sync points; expected is exactly equal to the median of the reported durations of the last 3 completed steps, and is frozen after entering the current step; gen_frac equals the previous step's generation fraction and remains constant for the entire step. Using progress to judge “how much longer” will mislead you the most on the slowest steps: pro step 15 progress hit 1.0 and then ran for another 3465 seconds, accounting for 26.9% of that step.
body: When the definition is not written clearly, people automatically assume that every number on the screen is “an observation of this very moment”. These three fields are not. progress is not calculated independently; it is just since ÷ expected and then truncated to 1; expected is also not a prediction for this step, but the median of the reported durations of the three most recently completed steps, and then it is not updated for the entire lifetime of the step; gen_frac is even more thorough—it describes what proportion of the previous step was generation, and it is the same number throughout the current step.

The verification method is to compare them by subtraction with the already-completed reported values in series.json, not to look at how they change over time. progress: compute since ÷ expected for each line of timeline.jsonl and compare it with the progress field; across the two runs there are 27 collection points, and the maximum absolute error is 0. expected: for each line, take the median reported duration of the most recent 3 steps when “completed up to step k”; 27/27 are exactly equal (error less than 0.05 seconds). gen_frac: for each line, take “previous step's outer_gen ÷ previous step's reported duration”; 27/27 are equal (error less than 1e-3).

The first practical consequence of this is that gen_frac cannot be used at all to answer “how far along is the generation for this step”. It is constant within this step; if you plot it as a curve, it is also a horizontal line. To determine whether the generation phase has ended, you can only look at the phase field flipping from rollout to training, and in practice this flip differs from the reported outer_gen by several hundred to over a thousand seconds (flash step 20: phase flips between since 3617.9~4824.0, reported outer_gen = 4932.0 seconds).

The second consequence is more costly: expected is backward-looking, and when step durations monotonically increase, it cannot keep up. Because progress = since/expected, the moment when “progress reaches 100%” also happens earlier. pro step 15 has progress = 1.0000 at since = 9416.4 seconds, but that step actually reported 12881.6 seconds—the last 3465.2 seconds (26.9%) displayed progress 100% and phase = training throughout. flash step 20 is the same; it was pinned at 100% for 1376.8 seconds (13.6%). Using this progress to schedule inspections or to judge “whether an eval can be inserted” will systematically miss the mark.

The third consequence is that it is not 'always' biased toward optimism. Using only non-restart steps, among pro's 17 steps, expected is optimistic on 8 and pessimistic on 9, median +0.13% (almost unbiased); among flash's 25 steps, it is optimistic on 16, median −1.57%. The real pattern is 'the distribution is very wide, both tails reach 30%, and the large errors on the optimistic side are concentrated on steps where the step length jumps up': pro's three most optimistic steps are −11.3% / −10.7% / −10.3%, flash's are −21.5% / −13.9% / −13.6%. So the correct judgment is 'the expected median is credible, the optimistic direction in the tail is not credible', not 'expected is systematically optimistic'—the latter is a judgment I wrote incorrectly in my own first draft and revised after recalculating.

A transferable practice: when you get any dashboard, first separate 'observed quantities' from 'derived quantities'. The criterion is simple—plug in the candidate derived formula; if the error is 0, then this field carries no new information, so don't build alerts on it; then do a distribution check on 'predictive' fields (expected, ETA, remaining time) to see whether their error is two-tailed or directional. Directional error is most dangerous when the load steps up.

items.title: The 'time gap' caused by restarts is not downtime: of the 5.63 hours missing at flash step 16, 3.96 hours are recomputation that ran to completion and was then discarded; the actual recovery wait is only 0.09 hours
items.summary: That timing_s/step does not include restart time has been said before, but treating the gap directly as 'wait' will get the accounting wrong. The gap can be split precisely into three things: the span from previous step completion to the last recovery, the overhead from recovery to step timer start, and recomputation discarded for whole steps. The third has one verifiable event in flash: steps 16 and 17 each completed once and were then rerun by redo, totaling 3.96 hours, equivalent to $40,728, while the actual recovery wait for this step is only 0.09 hours. There is also a directly usable constant: recovery overhead is 740~800 seconds per occurrence for pro and 328~367 seconds per occurrence for flash.
body: gap = true step duration (difference between adjacent axis.walls) − reported duration (timing_s/step). It has an exact identity: gap = (previous step completion → last recovery run) + (last recovery run → this step completion − this step's reported duration). The 11 gap steps across the two runs all match digit by digit, with error less than 0.001 seconds. The second term on the right-hand side is exactly the overhead of 'the new process has started, but the step timer has not yet started'; it can be measured precisely and is very stable.

First remember this constant: pro is 740.3~799.9 seconds each time (12.3~13.3 minutes), flash is 328.3~367.0 seconds each time (5.5~6.1 minutes). At their respective rates, for a single restart this invisible overhead alone is about $4,300 for pro and about $980 for flash. Its cause is not written in the data; in magnitude it looks like actions such as loading weights and rebuilding the data pipeline.

The first term on the right-hand side, 'previous step completion → last recovery run', is a mixed term: it contains both progress discarded before the crash and downtime from crash to recovery. Because the restart timestamp in events.json is **the moment the new process resumes running** (evidence: timeline's restarted_at equals it, and step.since is counted from it, matching point by point to within 1 second), the crash moment is unobservable, so this term cannot be separated across all 11 of pro's restarts.

flash step 16 is the only sample that can be separated. In events.json, steps 16 and 17 each appear twice, and the second occurrence carries redo=true, and announcement n-b60f90 says we restarted the flash run from step 15. Using the difference between the timestamps of adjacent step events, one can calculate that the first completions of these two steps took 6641.6 seconds and 7623.8 seconds respectively, totaling 14265.4 seconds = 3.96 hours, all invalidated. The gap for the same step is 20277.7 seconds, of which recovery overhead is only 332.1 seconds, and the remaining 5680.2 seconds is the span 'between the last completion and recovery'. So of the 5.63 hours missing from this step, the verifiable wasted compute is 3.96 hours, and the actual recovery waiting is 0.09 hours—a factor of 40 difference.

Counting the rerun itself as well, the cost of this incident is: 14265.4 seconds invalidated + 18193.1 seconds consumed by reruns (the reported value after rerunning steps 16 and 17) = 32458.5 seconds of extra machine time; relative to the counterfactual of "nothing ever went wrong", the extra wall clock spent is 24202 seconds = 6.72 hours, which at the flash rate of $2.855/second is $69,097.

A transferable rule of thumb: when you see the "downtime/failure time" metric definition, first ask whether it counts wall clock or billable time. In the wall-clock loss from a restart, recovery overhead is a constant term (you can directly multiply by the number of occurrences to get a lower bound), while discarded reruns are a conditional term (only events with a redo marker or a version rollback can prove them). The two are exactly equally expensive on the bill, but completely different for optimization—the former requires shortening the startup path; the latter requires changing "making intermediate results resumable, so that an entire step does not have to be redone." Mixing the two into a single "wait time" will make you spend your budget in the wrong place.

items.title: avg_staleness is a restart clock, not a load table: rank correlation with 'steps since last restart' is 0.944, and with actual step duration only −0.235
items.summary: Intuitively, 'steps get longer → trajectories don't finish → data gets stale' should hold; empirically this chain breaks in the middle. Getting longer is real, and getting staler is also real (flash step 24 has 9 staleness buckets, about 84% of the tokens come from 1 version earlier), but there is no association between the two: the rank correlation of avg_staleness with actual step duration is only pro −0.235, flash −0.070, while with 'steps since last restart' it is +0.944 / +0.885, and the rank correlation of bucket count with steps within a segment is 1.000 / 0.998. This metric is a restart clock, not a load table.
body: First rule out the mechanical identity: avg_staleness is exactly equal to Σ(k × frac_k), and point-by-point verification gives a maximum error of less than 1e-7. So it is not an independent observable itself; it is merely the weighted sum of the staleness bucket proportions, and when the proportions change, it changes. This must be stated clearly before judging causality.

Next look at what determines it. For each step, compute "how many steps have passed since the last restart" (position within the segment), and compute its rank correlation with avg_staleness: pro +0.944, flash +0.885. Correlation with the number of buckets: pro +0.944, flash +0.880. And the rank correlation of the number of buckets with position within the segment is pro 1.000, flash 0.998—that is, **after a restart, each step advanced adds one more bucket, without exception**. After each restart, pro's bucket count goes from 1 to 8, and flash's from 1 to 10.

Within the same set of samples, the rank correlation of avg_staleness with actual step duration is pro −0.235, flash −0.070; with average generation length it is −0.177 / +0.031; and with the current step's training tokens it is −0.226 / +0.045. All are near zero or slightly negative. If "longer steps make the data staler" held, there should be a significant positive correlation here.

So avg_staleness plotted out is a series of sawteeth; the start of each tooth is a restart (which zeroes the pipeline and replaces all data with the freshest), and the height of the tooth is how many versions accumulated in that segment. pro's three tooth peaks are 1.82 (step 9, reset at step 11), 1.21 (step 14, reset at step 15), 1.29 (step 22, reset at step 23); flash's are 1.89 (step 15, reset at step 16), 2.18 (step 24, reset at step 25), and the run ends when the final segment climbs to 1.19. **The more frequent the restarts, the "healthier" this metric looks, while it is actually just being zeroed out more often.**

This is not to say that staleness is unimportant. The magnitude of "data is very old" is itself large: at flash step 24, 84% of tokens come from at least one version earlier, and at pro step 9 it is 80.3%. Moreover, "steps getting longer" and "sandboxes being occupied longer" can be lined up on another chain: using Little's law to back out the average sandbox lifetime, pro rises from 1.198 hours (steps 3–10) to 1.793 hours (steps 17–22), and flash rises from 1.705 hours to 2.168 hours, in the same direction as the increase in generation length. So the correct statement is: long trajectories do create pressure in the system, but the pressure shows up in sandbox occupancy time, not in staleness.

Transferable judgment rule: for any "latency-type" metric, first find its reset event. For metrics whose reset is triggered by external events (restart, rollback, manual reset), their variance mainly comes from reset frequency; to measure the true effect of load on it, you must run the regression within the segment between two reset events, and treat "position within the segment" as a confounder that must be controlled for. Directly correlating it with load metrics over the full sample will give a conclusion with the completely opposite direction.

items.title: Backpressure counters are all identically 0 across two runs and 54 step observations: this layer is not blocked, and the long tail left no trace at this layer either
items.summary: Under train/trace, six overflow-type counters (backpressure wait count and seconds, orphan parsing, write failures, termination conflicts) are all 0 on pro 24 steps and flash 30 steps, with not one of 324 observation points nonzero. Drain wait drain_wait_seconds is at most 8.23 seconds, and outcome write outcome_write_seconds is at most 1.60 seconds; this layer never blocked the producer. The conclusion is negative but directly usable: optimization budget should not be spent here.
body: Backpressure is the most direct readout of queue overflow: when a bounded queue cannot be written to, the producer gets blocked, and "blocked" will definitely be counted. So to judge "whether this layer is the bottleneck," look at the number of non-zero occurrences of the overflow counter, not utilization or queue length. The train/trace family provides exactly this kind of counter, and the dashboard breaks it down very finely: wait count, wait seconds (sum, max), orphan resolution, write failures, termination conflicts.

The measured results are very clean: across pro's 24 steps and flash's 30 steps, these six items are all equal to 0, with not a single non-zero occurrence. The two accompanying items are also on the order of seconds: drain_wait_seconds is 1.29~8.23 seconds for pro and 2.55~5.87 seconds for flash; outcome_write_seconds is 0.46~1.60 seconds for pro and 0.52~0.85 seconds for flash. Placing these two numbers next to the 6,850~14,000-second step duration, the order of magnitude is one ten-thousandth to one thousandth.

There is one quantity that deserves attention but need not be over-interpreted: late_finishes is not 0; pro ranges from 0~47 (median 0, non-zero only at steps 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 21, and 22), flash ranges from 0~210 (median 14, with 17 of 30 steps non-zero). It is a count of "late completions," but the dashboard gives no definition and no accompanying wait seconds, so we can only note it: flash has more late completions than pro, consistent with that run having two full-step reruns (steps 16 and 17) and a longer context, but this is a coincidence-level consistency and cannot be treated as a conclusion.

Another timing coincidence worth recording: train/trace/records jumps from 1.63e6 to 3.27e6 at pro step 17, almost exactly doubling, and at the same moment writer_seconds_sum rises from about 5,000 seconds to about 8,000 seconds. Step 17 is exactly the step where that "expert load imbalance causing GPU OOM, adjusting the training parallelism strategy" restart occurred. This looks like the parallelism adjustment incidentally also changed the parallelism of trace writes, but the dashboard does not define these two fields; this article records it only as a clue.

Why it is worth writing a separate "nothing was found" entry: in this kind of system, "throughput being eaten by the long tail" is the most common narrative, and it will inevitably leave backpressure counts at some layer. This layer left none, which means the write-side buffer is large enough or the long tail was absorbed by concurrency (env/active runs on 20,000 to 38,000 sandboxes, and writes are asynchronous). The correct inference is "don't optimize here," not "there is no long tail."

Transferable judgment rule: to judge the bottleneck, look at two things together—the number of non-zero occurrences of the overflow counter, and the magnitude of drain/wait times. All 0 plus second-level waits equals "this layer has headroom"; once waits enter the minute level or the overflow count is non-zero, only then is it true backpressure. Conversely, high utilization does not mean blockage, and low utilization does not mean no blockage.

items.title: The upper bound of reward was pinned at 1 from step 1: max is exactly equal to 1 on pro 24/24 steps and flash 30/30 steps; only the middle rose
items.summary: critic/score/max has only one value 1.000 on pro 24/24 steps and flash 30/30 steps; "rewards concentrating toward a few high-scoring samples" cannot happen. critic/score/mean rises from 0.5522 to 0.5963 (pro, r=0.904) and from 0.5167 to 0.6005 (flash, r=0.939), with all changes in the middle of the distribution. Only the lower bound diverges: pro's mean−min narrows from 1.2593 to 0.7384, while flash expands from 1.3139 to 1.4005 (p=0.003).
body: On the dashboard, critic/score/max and critic/rewards/max are the same quantity (pointwise maximum absolute difference 0); it is "the trajectory with the highest score in this step's training batch". Intuitively one would assume that as training progresses → more good samples → max rises, but the data gives a simpler answer: max has been 1.000 since the first step, and did not change even once across 24 steps (pro) and 30 steps (flash). This indicates that the reward function has a hard upper bound, and the model was already able to reach it at the first step.

So any discussion about "changes in the shape of the reward distribution" can, in this data, only fall below max. Look at max−mean and mean−min separately: max−mean drops significantly in both runs (pro 0.4478→0.4037, r=−0.904, p=1.4e-9; flash 0.4833→0.3995, r=−0.939, p=1.8e-14) — this is a result of mean rising, not of max falling (max is constant at 1). mean−min is the quantity that actually carries direction: pro 1.2593→0.7384 (the worst samples are catching up to the mean, r=0.159, p=0.46 not significant but the magnitude is large), flash 1.3139→1.4005 (the worst samples fall further behind, r=0.523, p=0.003).

At the dataset level, this divergence is clearer: among pro's 23 datasets with data, 18 have first and last values of score/min both 0, while flash has only 7; pro has 3 datasets (code/bvg7, code/yfch, cyber/9aui) whose score/min touches −0.8 at least once, while flash has 6 (bvg7, obg8, v7yx, yfch, zg6q, cyber/9aui). In other words, the −0.8 floor of the global score/min is, on flash, a normal occurrence repeatedly triggered by multiple datasets, and on pro an occasional occurrence in a minority of datasets.

Chart-reading rule: when you see critic/score/max, first check whether it is constant. In this data it is the only constant (nDistinct=1), whereas critic/advantages/max is not (pro has 11 distinct values, flash has 13). To treat "max rising" as evidence of reward concentration, you must first rule out the possibility that "max is already at the upper bound" — once it is at the upper bound, the value of max no longer carries any information; all information is in mean and min.

Also note the cross-dataset non-additivity of critic/score/min: at pro step 14 the global min=−0.8000, whereas in the same period the min of the vast majority of datasets is 0.000; the −0.8 comes only from cyber/dataset-9aui (which itself only reports up to step 14). The global min is the minimum taken across 23 datasets; its jumps are essentially determined by a single dataset's single step, so do not use it to represent any subset.

items.title: Trainable pool contraction on flash offset 58% of the all-correct rate gain: a 0.1659 pool-share loss for a 0.1700 all-correct rate contribution
items.summary: Decomposed with avg@n = p1 + M·m: flash's trainable pool M drops from 0.7188 to 0.5528, all-correct rate rises from 0.1208 to 0.2907. Δavg@n=+0.1298 splits into all-correct rate +0.1700, pool contraction −0.0983, within-pool improvement +0.0582 (residual 0), pool contraction eats 58% of the all-correct rate gain; pro's pool barely moves (0.6759→0.6545), decomposing to +0.0236/−0.0125/+0.0207. pro's avg@n peaks at 0.6431 at step 20 then falls back to 0.5964.
body: The rule of dynamic sampling is to discard prompts that are all-correct and all-wrong — after subtracting the baseline within the group, the advantage of these two categories is identically zero, producing no gradient. So the stronger the model and the higher the all-correct rate, the smaller the trainable pool. This can be precisely quantified in this data, because the dashboard gives both p0 (dynsam/passrate/zero) and p1 (dynsam/passrate/one), and avg@n satisfies avg@n = p1 + M·m (M = 1−p0−p1), so the in-pool average pass rate m can be back-solved pointwise.

flash is a textbook case of this: M drops from 0.7188 to 0.5528, down 16.6 percentage points; the all-correct rate rises from 0.1208 to 0.2907 (a 2.4-fold increase); the in-pool pass rate rises from 0.5467 to 0.6382. After decomposing Δavg@n=+0.1298 into three terms, pool shrinkage contributes −0.0983, exactly eating 58% of the all-correct rate contribution +0.1700. The pro side is completely different: M only goes from 0.6759 to 0.6545, the all-correct rate from 0.1779 to 0.2014, and pool shrinkage deducts only 0.0125.

Here we need to correct a causal direction that is easy to get backwards. "Pool shrinkage causes avg@n growth to slow" sounds plausible, but arithmetically pool shrinkage is a negative term in Δavg@n; it makes avg@n lower, not the slope smaller. Slowing growth is a different matter, and in this data it cannot be detected in either run: regressing the point-by-point increments of avg@n on the increment index gives pro r=−0.305 (p=0.16), flash r=−0.076 (p=0.69). pro looks more like "peak then pullback" — step 20's 0.6431 is the highest over the whole run, after which four steps drop to 0.5964 (−7.3%), and the mean of the last 11 increments is negative.

What really deserves vigilance is "headroom being eaten by itself": flash still has 55% of the trainable pool left, pro still has 65%. If the all-correct rate continues to rise at the current speed, M will bottom out first, and by then avg@n will approach 1 but the training signal will be exhausted first. The direct readout for this risk is the relationship between M and avg@n — the level correlation is strong in both runs (pro r=−0.852 p=1.3e-7, flash r=−0.957 p=1.2e-16); after detrending, pro is still significant (r=−0.650, p=5.9e-4) while flash is not (r=−0.199, p=0.29), indicating that flash's relationship is mainly a common trend.

One definition that must be stated clearly: train/passrate/passrate_0_ratio and passrate_1_ratio look like "all-wrong rate / all-correct rate", but their denominator is the trajectories that entered the training batch, whereas the denominator of dynsam/passrate/* is the measured candidate pool. The two differ in value by an order of magnitude (pro's p0 is 0.0092→0.0389 versus 0.1462→0.1440), cannot be converted into each other, and the train/passrate pair cannot be used for the decomposition in this section.

items.title: Grading did not become more lenient: over 24 steps the five-dimensional rubric score fell from 4.4051 to 4.2902 (r=−0.874), the post-processing multiplier fell in tandem, while the grading completion rate and failure rate stayed flat throughout.
items.summary: The shape of the grading funnel did not change: groups_total and groups_judged trends are all not significant (p≥0.37); failure share of accepted pro 3.52%→4.16% (p=0.61); end2end_success_rate typically 0.94~0.97. But the scale for grading scores is tightening: equal-weight mean of the five-dimensional rubric score pro fell from 4.4051 to 4.2902 (r=−0.874), flash from 4.3919 to 4.3108. The “above reference solution” share select_above_gold_share is completely flat in pro (r=−0.003).
body: To answer "is grading getting looser or tighter", first separate two things: the throughput/health of the grading pipeline, and the scores the grader gives. The former can be verified directly with count-type metrics; the latter requires the grader's own absolute scores and post-processing coefficients.

On the throughput side, there is no change at all. The pro mean of groups_total is 1811 (n=24) and flash 1750 (n=30); their r against step number is −0.192 (p=0.37) and −0.004 (p=0.98) respectively; likewise for groups_judged (pro r=−0.094, p=0.66; flash r=0.053, p=0.78). The grading completion rate (groups_judged / groups_attempted) has pro mean 0.9498 and flash 0.9594, with no trend throughout. In the failed, skipped, and expired family, groups_failed_pass1/pass2, groups_skipped_unbalanced, groups_skipped_empty_inputs, judge_aux_missing_rollouts, keep_mass_capped, rollouts_masked, select_r2_capped_rate, dev_neg_turns, and select_r3_gold_fails are all identically zero in both runs; groups_expired_unjudged is 0 or 1 throughout pro, and in flash this tag does not even exist. The only low point in pro's end2end_success_rate is 0.7662 at step 14, which temporally matches the previous announcement (the network between the training cluster and the grading deployment was unreachable), and is a single-step infrastructure event.

On the scoring side, it is a different picture. The means of the five rubric dimensions A/B/E/P/S all have negative signs in both runs; among them, pro's E (r=−0.955, p=4.6e-13), B (r=−0.927), A (r=−0.787), and S (r=−0.640) are all significant, while flash's B (r=−0.710) and E (r=−0.628) are significant. After equal-weight averaging, pro drops from 4.4051 to 4.2902 (−0.1150), and flash goes from 4.3919 to 4.3108 (−0.0811). At the same time, select_factor_mean drops from 0.8319 to 0.8033 (pro), select_renorm_k_mean rises from 1.1852 to 1.2179, and select_renorm_capped_rate rises from 0.0346 to 0.0639 (r=0.574, p=0.003). These three point in the same direction: grading is being multiplied by a smaller factor, requires stronger renormalization compensation, and hits the renormalization cap more often.

So the hypothesis of “grading leniency” finds no supporting evidence in this dataset. Conversely, there is also no evidence that “the model truly surpassed the reference solution”—select_above_gold_share is completely flat over 24 steps on pro (r=−0.003, p=0.99), and the weak rise on flash (0.3018→0.3261, level r=0.377, p=0.040) does not hold under first differences (r=−0.341, p=0.071) or detrending (r=−0.058, p=0.76). To distinguish “capability improvement” from “grading relaxation”, the strongest evidence this dashboard can provide is that “the absolute scores of grading are moving in the tighter direction”, while the determination “surpassing the reference solution” itself lies in flatness or noise, and neither explanation can be ruled out.

An easily overlooked definitional fact: select_above_gold_share and select_v4/select_above_gold_share are exactly equal pointwise (maximum absolute difference 0), whereas under select_v4_nogold this field does not exist. That is, “exceeds the reference solution” is computed only on the grading path that has gold — this is its denominator basis, not a global proportion.

items.title: The grading probe inconsistency rate is at a high level of 0.586~0.606 and significantly rising, but over the same period the number of review red flags for “confirmed errors” is declining
items.summary: select_probe_disagree_rate is high and rising significantly: pro mean 0.6059 (0.5748→0.6331, p=2.1e-4), flash mean 0.5857 (0.5460→0.6018, p=1.4e-5). The external reading “grader inconsistency rate 60% and rising” can find a counterpart in this family; both magnitude and direction line up. But over the same period the review counts closer to “confirmed error” are declining: select_r2_flagged as a share of judged groups pro 0.3212→0.2080 (p=3.2e-5), flash 0.3129→0.2200.
body: select_probe_disagree_rate is the only metric in this dashboard that directly names “grader internal inconsistency.” It has no official definition; judging from its name and data shape, it is the proportion of cases where, during grading, multiple decision paths (probes) are used to verify the same batch of samples and the conclusions conflict. The mean over pro's 24 steps is 0.6059, and over flash's 30 steps is 0.5857, both around “sixty percent,” and both rise significantly with step number.

Compare the external readout item by item: the magnitude matches (0.586~0.606 vs “60%”), the direction matches (the p-values for the two runs are 2.1e-4 and 1.4e-5, respectively), and the existence also matches (this is not a metric that needs to be pieced together; the dashboard provides it directly). So that external readout is verifiable in this data.

But this cannot be read directly as “grading has collapsed.” On the same set of steps, counts that require multiple rounds of review to confirm are declining: the share of the completed-grading group held by select_r2_flagged falls for pro from 0.3212 to 0.2080 (r=−0.743), and for flash from 0.3129 to 0.2200 (r=−0.706); the share of the completed-grading group held by select_process_severe (graded as “severe process problem”) falls for flash from 0.0533 to 0.0188 (r=−0.545, p=0.002). Meanwhile, select_r1_masked's share of the completed-grading group is rising (pro 0.3822→0.4716, r=0.675; flash 0.3058→0.4515, r=0.542). That is: more disagreements appear in the first round and more samples need masking, but fewer need to reach a second round of review before being flagged red.

The most reasonable reading of this combination is “tasks became harder / samples are closer to the margin,” not “grading quality deteriorated” — but this is an inference, not directly proven by the data. The dashboard does not give a definition of probe_disagree, so “disagreement” cannot be equated with “misgrading”: for the same problem there are multiple reasonable solutions, so probe disagreement is inevitable.

There is also a methodological warning that must be written out: probe_disagree vs step is “a single series vs time,” with no object to detrend against, and monotonic trends over 24/30 points are naturally prone to producing significant results. When probe_disagree is correlated with avg@n, the level correlation looks strong (pro r=0.645, flash r=0.667); after first differencing, pro becomes −0.241 (p=0.27) and flash becomes −0.380 (p=0.042, significantly negative). So the reading that “grading disagreement rises as scores rise” does not hold in this data; the only thing that holds is “this readout itself is drifting.”
